claim: Orchestrated action of peptidoglycan (PG) synthetases and hydrolases is vital for bacterial growth and viability.
source: Orchestrated action of peptidoglycan (PG) synthetases and hydrolases is vital for bacterial growth and viability.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell wall biology.

claim: Many M23 family members can hydrolyse glycyl-glycine peptide bonds.
source: Many of these M23 family members can hydrolyse glycyl-glycine peptide bonds and show lytic activity against Staphylococcus aureus whose PG contains a pentaglycine bridge, but their exact substrate specificity and hydrolysed bonds are still vaguely determined.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about M23 family enzymes.

claim: M23 family members show lytic activity against Staphylococcus aureus whose PG contains a pentaglycine bridge.
source: Many of these M23 family members can hydrolyse glycyl-glycine peptide bonds and show lytic activity against Staphylococcus aureus whose PG contains a pentaglycine bridge, but their exact substrate specificity and hydrolysed bonds are still vaguely determined.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about M23 family enzymes.

claim: The exact substrate specificity and hydrolysed bonds of M23 family members are still vaguely determined.
source: Many of these M23 family members can hydrolyse glycyl-glycine peptide bonds and show lytic activity against Staphylococcus aureus whose PG contains a pentaglycine bridge, but their exact substrate specificity and hydrolysed bonds are still vaguely determined.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The substrate specificities of LytM and lysostaphin are similar.
source: Indeed, our results show that the substrate specificities of these structurally highly homologous enzymes are similar, but unlike observed earlier both LytM and lysostaphin prefer the D-Ala-Gly cross-linked part of mature peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the NMR spectroscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Both LytM and lysostaphin prefer the D-Ala-Gly cross-linked part of mature peptidoglycan.
source: Indeed, our results show that the substrate specificities of these structurally highly homologous enzymes are similar, but unlike observed earlier both LytM and lysostaphin prefer the D-Ala-Gly cross-linked part of mature peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the NMR spectroscopy experiments and kinetic measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: Lysostaphin is genuinely a glycyl-glycine hydrolase.
source: However, we show that while lysostaphin is genuinely a glycyl-glycine hydrolase, LytM can also act as a D-alanyl-glycine endopeptidase.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the NMR spectroscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: LytM can act as a D-alanyl-glycine endopeptidase.
source: However, we show that while lysostaphin is genuinely a glycyl-glycine hydrolase, LytM can also act as a D-alanyl-glycine endopeptidase.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the NMR spectroscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Multi-resistant bacteria pose a serious threat to global health.
source: In the age of antibiotic resistance, multi-resistant bacteria pose a serious threat to global health. This calls for novel strategies to fight the infections (Shrivastava et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shrivastava et al., 2018.

claim: One of the most common mechanisms of action of antibiotics is inhibition of the peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis.
source: One of the most common mechanisms of action of antibiotics is inhibition of the peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis, a major macromolecular structure in the bacterial cell wall (Džidić et al., 2008; Kapoor et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Džidić et al., 2008 and Kapoor et al., 2017.

claim: Peptidoglycan is a major macromolecular structure in the bacterial cell wall.
source: One of the most common mechanisms of action of antibiotics is inhibition of the peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis, a major macromolecular structure in the bacterial cell wall (Džidić et al., 2008; Kapoor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is notorious in developing resistance towards β-lactam-based antibiotics.
source: Alarmingly, the Gram-positive bacterium Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is notorious in developing resistance towards β-lactam-based antibiotics, e.g., penicillin and their derivatives, which target penicillin binding proteins that are vital for PG synthesis (Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sauvage et al., 2008.

claim: β-lactam-based antibiotics target penicillin binding proteins that are vital for PG synthesis.
source: Alarmingly, the Gram-positive bacterium Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is notorious in developing resistance towards β-lactam-based antibiotics, e.g., penicillin and their derivatives, which target penicillin binding proteins that are vital for PG synthesis (Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sauvage et al., 2008.

claim: Methicillin-resistant strains of S. aureus (MRSA) can cause life-threatening infections which are very difficult to eradicate.
source: These methicillin-resistant strains of S. aureus (MRSA) can cause life-threatening infections which are very difficult to eradicate (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: Outbreaks of infections caused by vancomycin intermediate-level and fully resistant S. aureus are lurking on the horizon.
source: Moreover, although still rarely occurring, outbreaks of infections caused by vancomycin intermediate-level and fully resistant S. aureus are lurking on the horizon (Shariati et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shariati et al., 2020.

claim: Cell division, cell shape determination, PG remodelling, and recycling are coordinated and executed by peptidoglycan hydrolases (PGHs).
source: Cell division, cell shape determination, PG remodelling, and recycling are coordinated and executed by peptidoglycan hydrolases (PGHs), enzymes produced to function as (auto)lysins in the regulation of the cell wall during growth and division (Ghuysen, 1968; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghuysen, 1968 and Wang et al., 2022.

claim: Lysostaphin (LSS) is an exolysin secreted by Staphylococcus simulans biovar staphylolyticus.
source: On the other hand, PGHs may also function as defensive weapons against other bacterial species as in the case of lysostaphin (LSS), an exolysin secreted by Staphylococcus simulans biovar staphylolyticus, which displays bactericidal action against competing S. aureus (Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964.

claim: Lysostaphin displays bactericidal action against competing S. aureus.
source: On the other hand, PGHs may also function as defensive weapons against other bacterial species as in the case of lysostaphin (LSS), an exolysin secreted by Staphylococcus simulans biovar staphylolyticus, which displays bactericidal action against competing S. aureus (Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964.

claim: The potential antibacterial role of PGHs is based on the targeted destruction of the protecting PG by hydrolysis, which leads to lysis of the bacterial cells upon increasing turgor pressure.
source: The potential antibacterial role of PGHs is based on the targeted destruction of the protecting PG by hydrolysis, which leads to lysis of the bacterial cells upon increasing turgor pressure (Ghuysen, 1968; Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghuysen, 1968 and Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964.

claim: PGHs are promising bactericins as well as druggable targets for the treatment of multidrug-resistant S. aureus infections.
source: Given that PGHs are promising bactericins as well as druggable targets for the treatment of multidrug-resistant S. aureus infections, profound knowledge of their structure, function, as well as substrate specificity is instrumental to harness their full potential as a new breed of antibiotics (Szweda et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Szweda et al., 2012.

claim: S. aureus and other Gram-positive bacteria are protected by a thick PG layer that is composed of repeating β-1,4-linked N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) and N-acetylglucosamine disaccharide units.
source: S. aureus and other Gram-positive bacteria are protected by a thick PG layer that is composed of repeating β-1,4-linked N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) and N-acetylglucosamine disaccharide units, forming the conserved glycan backbone of murein (Ghuysen, 1968; Schleifer and Kandler, 1972; Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghuysen, 1968 and Schleifer and Kandler, 1972, and references Figure 1A, B.

claim: In S. aureus the cross-bridge is characteristically composed of five glycine residues.
source: In S. aureus the cross-bridge is characteristically composed of five glycine residues (Ghuysen, 1968).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ghuysen, 1968.

claim: Cross-bridging provides an integral structural support for the entire PG wall and allows PG to reach a thickness of over 40 layers (20–80 nm) in Gram-positive bacterial species.
source: Cross-bridging provides an integral structural support for the entire PG wall and allows PG to reach a thickness of over 40 layers (20–80 nm) in Gram-positive bacterial species (Ghuysen, 1968; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghuysen, 1968 and Kim et al., 2015.

claim: LytM and LSS both belong to the zinc-dependent M23 family of metalloendopeptidases.
source: Here, we compared LytM and LSS, which both belong to the zinc-dependent M23 family of metalloendopeptidases and are designated as glycyl-glycine hydrolases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of these enzymes.

claim: LytM and LSS are designated as glycyl-glycine hydrolases.
source: Here, we compared LytM and LSS, which both belong to the zinc-dependent M23 family of metalloendopeptidases and are designated as glycyl-glycine hydrolases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of these enzymes.

claim: LytM and LSS have been shown to cleave the peptide bonds between glycine residues in the pentaglycine cross-bridge of S. aureus PG.
source: They have been shown to cleave the peptide bonds between glycine residues in the pentaglycine cross-bridge of S. aureus PG (Figure 1B; Bardelang et al., 2009; Browder et al., 1965; Iversen and Grov, 1973; Odintsov et al., 2004; Ramadurai et al., 1999; Raulinaitis et al., 2017; Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964; Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964; Tossavainen et al., 2018; Warfield et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and references Figure 1B.

claim: S. simulans LSS is an exolysin possessing bacteriolytic properties towards staphylococci with a pentaglycine cross-bridge structure.
source: S. simulans LSS is an exolysin possessing bacteriolytic properties towards staphylococci with a pentaglycine cross-bridge structure, e.g., S. aureus, S. carnosus, S. cohnii (Grabowska et al., 2015; Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964; Schleifer and Fischer, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grabowska et al., 2015, Schindler and Schuhardt, 1964, and Schleifer and Fischer, 1982.

claim: LytM is a S. aureus PG hydrolase with a catalytic M23 domain structurally very similar to that of LSS.
source: LytM is a S. aureus PG hydrolase with a catalytic M23 domain structurally very similar to that of LSS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement references Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing structural similarity.

claim: The common fold of M23 enzymes consists of a characteristic narrow groove formed by a β sheet and four surrounding loops.
source: The common fold consists of a characteristic narrow groove formed by a β sheet and four surrounding loops.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of M23 enzymes based on established knowledge.

claim: At one end of the groove resides the catalytic site in which a zinc cation is coordinated by two conserved histidines and an aspartate.
source: At one end of the groove resides the catalytic site in which a zinc cation is coordinated by two conserved histidines and an aspartate.
evidence: This is a description of the catalytic mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: The zinc cation polarises the peptide bond and a nucleophilic water molecule activated by two other conserved histidines act in concert to hydrolyse the substrate glycyl-glycine bond.
source: The zinc cation, which polarises the peptide bond, and a nucleophilic water molecule activated by two other conserved histidines act in concert to hydrolyse the substrate glycyl-glycine bond (Grabowska et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grabowska et al., 2015.

claim: Browder et al. reported LSS cleavage between glycines 4 and 5.
source: Indeed, the exact cross-bridge bond that LSS targets remains controversial; Browder et al. reported LSS cleavage between glycines 4 and 5 while Sloan and colleagues observed cleavage of all glycyl-glycine bonds with several substrates of different sizes (Browder et al., 1965; Sloan et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Browder et al., 1965.

claim: Sloan and colleagues observed cleavage of all glycyl-glycine bonds with several substrates of different sizes.
source: Indeed, the exact cross-bridge bond that LSS targets remains controversial; Browder et al. reported LSS cleavage between glycines 4 and 5 while Sloan and colleagues observed cleavage of all glycyl-glycine bonds with several substrates of different sizes (Browder et al., 1965; Sloan et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sloan et al., 1977.

claim: Using mass spectrometry (MS), Schneewind and colleagues observed LSS-mediated cleavage between glycines 3 and 4.
source: Using mass spectrometry (MS), Schneewind and colleagues observed LSS-mediated cleavage between glycines 3 and 4 (Schneewind et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schneewind et al., 1995.

claim: A recent NMR spectroscopic study highlighted that hydrolysis by LSS produced fragments in which either two or three glycines are interlinked to the lysine sidechain.
source: This observation was supported by a recent NMR spectroscopic study highlighting that hydrolysis by LSS produced fragments in which either two or three glycines are interlinked to the lysine sidechain (Maya-Martinez et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maya-Martinez et al., 2018.

claim: Xu and coworkers reported cleavage at several sites with digested muropeptides: between glycines 1 and 2, 2 and 3, as well as 3 and 4.
source: On the other hand, Xu and coworkers reported cleavage at several sites with digested muropeptides: between glycines 1 and 2, 2 and 3, as well as 3 and 4 (Xu et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 1997.

claim: Studies carried out with FRET peptides reported cleavage between glycines 2 and 3 (~60 %) and glycines 3 and 4 (~40%).
source: Moreover, studies carried out with FRET peptides reported cleavage between glycines 2 and 3 (~60 %) and glycines 3 and 4 (~40%) (Warfield et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Warfield et al., 2006.

claim: LytM has been shown to hydrolyse pGly into di- and triglycine, and tetraglycine into diglycine.
source: LytM has been shown to hydrolyse pGly into di- and triglycine, and tetraglycine into diglycine (Firczuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Firczuk et al., 2005.

claim: LSS hydrolyses pGly 15-fold faster than LytM in vitro.
source: Results indicate that LSS hydrolyses pGly 15-fold faster than LytM in vitro (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OD600 of late stationary cells reduced from 100% to 25% in 1.5 and 12 hr for LSS and LytM, respectively.
source: These data show that OD600 of late stationary cells reduced from 100% to 25% in 1.5 and 12 hr for LSS and LytM, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on turbidity reduction assay data.

claim: LytM and LSS are highly specific for the bond between Gly2 and Gly3 (>85–94%).
source: These data clearly show that LytM and LSS are highly specific for the bond between Gly2 and Gly3 (>85–94%, Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Residual cleavage activity towards the bond between Gly3 and Gly4 is evident (<15%) for LytM and LSS.
source: However, residual cleavage activity towards the bond between Gly3 and Gly4 is also evident (<15%).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: Cross-linking L-Lys-D-Ala dipeptide N-terminally to pGly in 2 increased the rate of hydrolysis with respect to 1 by a factor of 12 and 8 for LSS and LytM, respectively.
source: Indeed, cross-linking L-Lys-D-Ala dipeptide N-terminally to pGly in 2 increased the rate of hydrolysis with respect to 1 by a factor of 12 and 8 for LSS and LytM, respectively (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Further elongation in the N-terminus (ADiQKDA-GGGGG, 3) had only incremental contribution to the rate of overall substrate hydrolysis, 17 and 3 for LSS and LytM, respectively.
source: Further elongation in the N-terminus (ADiQKDA-GGGGG, 3) had only incremental contribution to the rate of overall substrate hydrolysis, 17 and 3 for LSS and LytM, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: For LSS, the rate of hydrolysis increased by six- and fivefold for substrates 4 and 5, respectively.
source: For LSS, the rate of hydrolysis increased by six- and fivefold for substrates 4 and 5, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: For LytM, activity towards PG fragments 4 and 5 is only 82% and 72%, respectively, of that found for 1.
source: For LytM, the outcome was in stark contrast to the results observed with LSS. Indeed, LytM activity towards PG fragments 4 and 5 is only 82% and 72%, respectively, of that found for 1.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: For LSS, 10-fold rate enhancements with respect to 1 for substrate hydrolysis were observed for substrates 6 and 7.
source: For LSS, 10-fold rate enhancements with respect to 1 for substrate hydrolysis were observed, comparable to enhancements with substrates 2 and 3, indicating that the moiety C-terminal to pGly does not contribute to LSS catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: Rate enhancements of PG fragments 6 and 7 with respect to 1 were 5.5- and 3.5-fold, respectively, for LytM.
source: In the case of LytM, rate enhancements of PG fragments 6 and 7 with respect to 1 were 5.5- and 3.5-fold, respectively, meaning that the branched stem peptide linked to the C-terminal end of pGly has a slight negative effect on LytM activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: LytM as well as LSS prefer mature PG fragments as substrates i.e., PG units that contain a D-Ala-Gly cross-link between two stem peptides.
source: In all, overall rates of substrate hydrolysis using comparative real-time kinetics convincingly indicate that LytM as well as LSS prefer mature PG fragments as substrates i.e., PG units that contain a D-Ala-Gly cross-link between two stem peptides.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: In substrate 2, LSS hydrolyses amide bonds between Gly1-Gly2 and Gly2-Gly3 with a clear preference for the first one.
source: These data show that in 2 LSS hydrolyses amide bonds between Gly1-Gly2 and Gly2-Gly3 with a clear preference for the first one.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: LytM is able to cleave the D-Ala-Gly1 amide bond in the S. aureus PG cross-bridge whenever the cross-linked D-Ala-Gly structure is available.
source: Indeed, given that LytM is a well-established glycyl-glycine endopeptidase (Firczuk et al., 2005; Grabowska et al., 2015; Ramadurai et al., 1999), we were taken by surprise to observe that LytM, in addition to Gly1-Gly2 bond hydrolysis, is also able to cleave the D-Ala-Gly1 amide bond in the S. aureus PG cross-bridge whenever the cross-linked D-Ala-Gly structure is available.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: LytM belongs to a small family of endopeptidases which cleave the peptide bond between D-Ala and Gly.
source: The results confirm that in addition to being a glycyl-glycine endopeptidase as reported earlier (Firczuk et al., 2005; Grabowska et al., 2015; Ramadurai et al., 1999), LytM belongs to a small family of endopeptidases which cleave the peptide bond between D-Ala and Gly.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data and comparison with inactive mutant.

claim: In substrates 2 and 6 LytM cleaves between D-Ala-Gly and Gly1-Gly2 with approximately equal rates.
source: In substrates 2 and 6 LytM cleaves between D-Ala-Gly and Gly1-Gly2 with approximately equal rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: For the N-terminally longer substrates 3 and 7, the balance is shifted in favour of hydrolysis of Gly1-Gly2 for LytM.
source: For the N-terminally longer substrates 3 and 7, the balance is shifted in favour of hydrolysis of Gly1-Gly2.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: LytM strongly favoured D-Ala-Gly cleavage in 13 (KDAGGG) whereas it preferred Gly1-Gly2 cleavage in 12 (KDAGGGG).
source: However, LytM strongly favoured D-Ala-Gly cleavage in 13 (KDAGGG) whereas it preferred Gly1-Gly2 cleavage in 12 (KDAGGGG).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: LytM can hydrolyse 14 (KDAGG) and only the D-alanyl-glycine bond is cleaved.
source: Unlike LSS, LytM can still hydrolyse 14 (KDAGG). Only the D-alanyl-glycine bond is cleaved, and the reaction is five to ten times slower than hydrolysis of 2, 12, and 13.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: LSS hydrolyses the peptide bond between Gly1 and Gly2 in muropeptides extracted from S. aureus USA300 sacculus.
source: LSS hydrolyses the peptide bond between Gly1 and Gly2, recognised as the appearance of interconnected C-terminal Gly1 1Hα-13CO and D-Ala 1Hα-13CO peaks in the 13C-HMBC spectrum (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: LytM hydrolyses the amide bond between Gly1 and Gly2 in muropeptides extracted from S. aureus USA300 sacculus.
source: Identical correlations are observed for LytM, indicating that it also hydrolyses the amide bond between Gly1 and Gly2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: LytM is cutting both glycyl-glycine and D-alanyl-glycine bonds in muropeptides extracted from S. aureus sacculus.
source: This indicates that LytM is cutting both glycyl-glycine and D-alanyl-glycine bonds also in muropeptides extracted from S. aureus sacculus.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: FemX, FemA, and FemB catalyse nonribosomal insertion of mono-(Gly5), di-(Gly4-Gly3), and di-(Gly2-Gly1) glycines into the glycine cross-bridge in S. aureus PG, respectively.
source: For instance, gene products of fem (factor essential to methicillin resistance) family members, i.e., FemX, FemA, and FemB catalyse nonribosomal insertion of mono-(Gly5), di-(Gly4-Gly3), and di-(Gly2-Gly1) glycines into the glycine cross-bridge in S. aureus PG, respectively (Gründling et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gründling et al., 2006.

claim: Reduced susceptibility of S. aureus ΔfemB and ΔfemAB mutant strains towards LSS has been observed earlier.
source: Reduced susceptibility of S. aureus ΔfemB and ΔfemAB mutant strains towards LSS has been observed earlier (Małecki et al., 2021; Strandén et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Małecki et al., 2021 and Strandén et al., 1997.

claim: LSS hydrolyses substrate 8 with an increased rate as compared to 7.
source: Interestingly, LSS hydrolyses 8 with an increased rate as compared to 7 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LSS is able to hydrolyse substrate 9, devoid of glycyl-glycine bond, by hydrolysing the Lys Nζ-monoGly CO isopeptide bond.
source: Quite surprisingly, we also observed that LSS is able to hydrolyse substrate 9, devoid of glycyl-glycine bond. Instead, LSS hydrolyses the Lys Nζ-monoGly CO isopeptide bond.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rate of hydrolysis of substrate 9 by LSS is drastically lower (1.2%) than that of the amide bond between glycines in 7.
source: The rate of hydrolysis is, however, drastically lower (1.2%) than that of the amide bond between glycines in 7 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Lytic efficiency of LSS against ΔfemB mutant is not drastically reduced while the minimum inhibitory concentration is three orders of magnitude higher for the ΔfemAB mutant.
source: Indeed, lytic efficiency of LSS against ΔfemB mutant is not drastically reduced while the minimum inhibitory concentration is three orders of magnitude higher for the ΔfemAB mutant (Gründling et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gründling et al., 2006.

claim: Even if the number of glycines in the cross-bridge is reduced from five to three, LytM is still able to hydrolyse both D-Ala-Gly and glycyl-glycine bonds.
source: Similar results were obtained with LytM except for the scissile bond specificity. Even if the number of glycines in the cross-bridge is reduced from five to three, LytM is still able to hydrolyse both D-Ala-Gly and glycyl-glycine bonds (sites '1' or '5') (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: If stem peptides are cross-linked with only a single glycine in the cross-bridge (9), LytM displays diminished activity by eightfold in comparison to 7.
source: However, if stem peptides are cross-linked with only a single glycine in the cross-bridge (9), LytM displays diminished activity by eightfold in comparison to 7.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data.

claim: LytM hydrolysed the Lys Nζ -monoGly CO isopeptide bond in substrate 9.
source: Yet somewhat surprisingly, considering the cleavage of D-Ala-Gly bond in substrate 14 (KDAGG, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), LytM hydrolysed the Lys Nζ -monoGly CO isopeptide bond.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: Of the two PG fragments 10 and 11, having Gly2 or Gly3 replaced by a serine, only 11 was hydrolysed by LSS.
source: Of the two PG fragments 10 and 11, having Gly2 or Gly3 replaced by a serine, only 11 was hydrolysed by LSS.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: LSS cleaved the bond between Gly1 and Gly2 in 11 although with a rate 30-fold slower than that for substrate 2.
source: LSS cleaved the bond between Gly1 and Gly2 in 11 although with a rate 30-fold slower than that for substrate 2 (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: LytM was able to hydrolyse both PG fragments 10 and 11.
source: LytM was able to hydrolyse both PG fragments.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: LytM specifically cleaved the D-Ala-Gly amide bond in 10 as it contains serine in the second position.
source: 11 was cleaved similarly to the PG fragment 2, whereas LytM specifically cleaved the D-Ala-Gly amide bond in 10 as it contains serine in the second position.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rates of substrate hydrolysis for LytM were not drastically lower, i.e., by a factor of 4.3 (10) and 1.5 (11) in comparison to 2.
source: The rates of substrate hydrolysis were not drastically lower, i.e., by a factor of 4.3 (10) and 1.5 (11) in comparison to 2 (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on NMR kinetics data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: LSS is a glycyl-glycine endopeptidase as P1 and P1' positions are invariably occupied by Gly residues.
source: It is clear that LSS is a glycyl-glycine endopeptidase as P1 and P1' positions are invariably occupied by Gly residues (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The rate of hydrolysis by LSS increases when D-Ala occupies the P2 position.
source: However, the rate of hydrolysis increases when D-Ala occupies the P2 position, i.e., when LSS recognises a D-Ala-Gly cross-link in the cell wall.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: LytM is flexible regarding the P1 site, it can be accommodated either by D-Ala or Gly, whereas the P1' position is invariably occupied by Gly.
source: LytM is flexible regarding the P1 site, it can be accommodated either by D-Ala or Gly, whereas the P1' position is invariably occupied by Gly (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: D-Ala in the P1/S1 position in the LSS active site results in a steric clash with loop 1, most notably its residues L272-I274, thus preventing hydrolysis of a D-alanyl-glycine peptide bond.
source: D-Ala in the P1/S1 position in the LSS active site results in a steric clash with loop 1, most notably its residues L272-I274, thus preventing hydrolysis of a D-alanyl-glycine peptide bond (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In LytM the corresponding loop is shorter allowing accommodation of D-Ala in the P1/S1 position and hence cleavage of D-alanyl-glycine cross-bridge.
source: In LytM the corresponding loop is shorter allowing accommodation of D-Ala in the P1/S1 position and hence cleavage of D-alanyl-glycine cross-bridge or alternatively, if the substrate has a Gly in the P1 position, the peptide bond between Gly1 and Gly2 (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 5D and F.

claim: Serine in the P2' position severely hinders accommodation of the substrate to the LSS active site, which results in a drastic drop in the rate of hydrolysis.
source: The same loop 1 gates the LSS active site and establishes the structural basis for Lif function. Serine in the P2' position severely hinders accommodation of the substrate to the LSS active site, which results in a drastic drop in the rate of hydrolysis (Figure 5A and G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on molecular modeling and kinetic data shown in Figure 5A and G.

claim: In LytM the three residues shorter loop renders the active site more voluminous, which permits the short polar sidechain of Ser to fit into the P2' or P3' positions.
source: In LytM the three residues shorter loop renders the active site more voluminous, which permits the short polar sidechain of Ser to fit into the P2' or P3' positions (Figure 5B and H–J).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 5B and H–J.

claim: Substrates 10 (KDAGSGGG) and 11 (KDAGGSGG) can be hydrolysed by LytM with relatively high efficiency (ca. 50%) in comparison to PG fragment 2 which contains a pGly bridge.
source: Consequently, substrates 10 (KDAGSGGG) and 11 (KDAGGSGG) can still be hydrolysed with relatively high efficiency (ca. 50%) in comparison to PG fragment 2 which contains a pGly bridge (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinetic data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the D-Ala-Gly cross-link is missing, the cleavage site is shifted within the glycine cross-bridge, i.e., cutting occurs between Gly2 and Gly3.
source: Interestingly, when the D-Ala-Gly cross-link is missing, e.g., in pGly or PG fragments 4 and 5, the latter mimicking a non-cross-linked PG monomer, the cleavage site is shifted within the glycine cross-bridge, i.e., cutting occurs between Gly2 and Gly3 since in minimum a substrate with four residues occupying P2, P1, P1', and P2' sites is required for both LSS and LytM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: A substrate with four residues occupying P2, P1, P1', and P2' sites is required for both LSS and LytM.
source: Interestingly, when the D-Ala-Gly cross-link is missing, e.g., in pGly or PG fragments 4 and 5, the latter mimicking a non-cross-linked PG monomer, the cleavage site is shifted within the glycine cross-bridge, i.e., cutting occurs between Gly2 and Gly3 since in minimum a substrate with four residues occupying P2, P1, P1', and P2' sites is required for both LSS and LytM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: Only LytM can cleave 14 (KDAGG) since it accepts D-Ala in the P1 position.
source: Owing to this limitation in substrate size and distinct difference in the substrate specificity of LSS and LytM, we observe that while both enzymes can hydrolyse tetraglycine, only LytM can cleave 14 (KDAGG) since it accepts D-Ala in the P1 position.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: Significant reduction in rate of hydrolysis for both LSS and LytM occurs when the substrate is too short, i.e., it cannot fill the P3'/S3' position.
source: We observed significant reduction in rate of hydrolysis for both LSS and LytM when the substrate is too short, i.e., it cannot fill the P3'/S3' position.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic data.

claim: The reduction in rate when substrate is too short is probably due to the stabilising hydrogen bonds that are formed between the longer glycine chain and a key asparagine residue in loop 4, Asn372 and Asn303 for LSS and LytM, respectively.
source: This is probably due to the stabilising hydrogen bonds that are formed between the longer glycine chain and a key asparagine residue in loop 4, Asn372 and Asn303 for LSS and LytM, respectively (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: LSS recognises the D-Ala-Gly cross-link and in such a substrate, D-Ala occupies the P2 position, which increases the rate of hydrolysis by 10-fold in comparison to substrates which position glycine into P2.
source: Our data also explain the inconsistencies between results of previous studies, i.e., our extensive set of PG fragments allowed a more comprehensive interpretation than previous studies with fewer substrates (Bardelang et al., 2009; Browder et al., 1965; Gründling et al., 2006; Małecki et al., 2021; Maya-Martinez et al., 2018; Reste de Roca et al., 2010; Sabala et al., 2014; Schneewind et al., 1995; Sloan et al., 1977; Warfield et al., 2006; Xu et al., 1997). LSS recognises the D-Ala-Gly cross-link. In such a substrate, D-Ala occupies the P2 position, which increases the rate of hydrolysis by 10-fold in comparison to substrates which position glycine into P2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the kinetic data shown in Figure 5.

claim: LSS prefers cutting between Gly1 and Gly2, whenever Gly1 is cross-linked to D-Ala of neighbouring stem, whereas it hydrolyses the amide bond between Gly2 and Gly3 in non-cross-linked (devoid of D-Ala-Gly bond) PG fragments.
source: To summarise, LSS prefers cutting between Gly1 and Gly2, whenever Gly1 is cross-linked to D-Ala of neighbouring stem, whereas it hydrolyses the amide bond between Gly2 and Gly3 in non-cross-linked (devoid of D-Ala-Gly bond) PG fragments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: LytM was originally categorised as a glycyl-glycine endopeptidase based on lytic experiments performed using purified cell walls.
source: LytM was originally categorised as a glycyl-glycine endopeptidase based on lytic experiments performed using purified cell walls, which showed that it is active against S. aureus and S. carnosus but not against Micrococcus luteus (Ramadurai et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ramadurai et al., 1999.

claim: M. luteus PG has the following structure: Ala-(D-γGlu-Gly)-Lys[D-Ala-Lys-D-Glu(-Gly)-Ala-D-Ala-Lys-D-γGlu(-Gly)-Ala]-D-Ala and thus contains neither Gly-Gly nor D-Ala-Gly bonds.
source: M. luteus PG has the following structure: Ala-(D-γGlu-Gly)-Lys[D-Ala-Lys-D-Glu(-Gly)-Ala-D-Ala-Lys-D-γGlu(-Gly)-Ala]-D-Ala and thus contains neither Gly-Gly nor D-Ala-Gly bonds (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: The only other recognised D-Ala-Gly hydrolase in S. aureus is LytN.
source: The only other recognised D-Ala-Gly hydrolase in S. aureus is LytN.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about S. aureus enzymes.

claim: LytN contains a catalytic CHAP domain, which cleaves both D-Ala-Gly and MurNAc-L-Ala bonds.
source: Contrary to LytM, it contains a catalytic CHAP domain, which cleaves both D-Ala-Gly and MurNAc-L-Ala bonds, in other words is a D-alanyl-glycine endopeptidase as well as an N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine amidase domain (Frankel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Frankel et al., 2011.

claim: D-Ala-Gly cleavage activity has been found from a CHAP domain of a S. aureus Phage ϕ11 murein hydrolase.
source: D-Ala-Gly cleavage activity has also been found from a CHAP domain of a S. aureus Phage ϕ11 murein hydrolase. In this hydrolase amidase activity is contained in another domain of the modular protein (Sabala et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sabala et al., 2014.

claim: Enterococcus faecalis EnpA, which belongs to the M23 metalloendopeptidase family, has been shown to cleave D-Ala-Ala bond in E. faecalis.
source: Recently also Enterococcus faecalis EnpA, which belongs to the M23 metalloendopeptidase family, has been shown to cleave D-Ala-Ala bond in E. faecalis.
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings on EnpA.

claim: EnpA exhibits substrate specificity similar to that of LytM, which allows occupation of the P1 position by D-Ala (and Gly).
source: Given that the P1 site in EnpA can accommodate D-Ala, it exhibits substrate specificity similar to that of LytM, which allows occupation of the P1 position by D-Ala (and Gly).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: Similar to LSS, LytM allows only glycine at the P1' site, whereas EnpA is more promiscuous and can accommodate Gly, L-Ala, and L-Ser in this position.
source: On the other hand, similar to LSS, LytM allows only glycine at the P1' site, whereas EnpA is more promiscuous and can accommodate Gly, L-Ala, and L-Ser in this position (Małecki et al., 2021; Reste de Roca et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Małecki et al., 2021 and Reste de Roca et al., 2010.

claim: The substrate specificity of LSS is defined by the D-Ala-Gly cross-link, which increases catalytic efficiency 10-fold with respect to pentaglycine.
source: Yet, we show for the first time that the substrate specificity of LSS is defined by the D-Ala-Gly cross-link, which increases catalytic efficiency 10-fold with respect to pentaglycine.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the kinetic data.
